passages.happening:
Micah speaks to the leaders of Jacob and the rulers of Israel. ‘Should you not know justice?’ (verse 1). They hate good and love evil (verse 2). Micah pictures them treating the people as a butcher treats meat for the pot (verses 2-3). These notes name the picture and do not repeat it.

When disaster comes they will cry out to the LORD, but he will not answer them. He will hide his face from them, because of the evil they have done (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
The chapter reflects Jerusalem in the late eighth century, under Ahaz and Hezekiah. The city was growing fast, partly with refugees from the north, and great building projects were under way; archaeologists have found evidence of Jerusalem spreading onto the western hill in this period, and Hezekiah's tunnel and fortifications belong to it.

Rulers and elders judged cases at the city gate and in the royal courts, and the law demanded fair judgment. These men should have known justice. Instead, Micah says, they fed on the people. The picture is grotesque on purpose. It is not literal cannibalism but a way of saying that those meant to protect the weak were consuming them.

The judgment matches the crime. They would not hear the cry of the poor. God will not hear theirs.
passages.later: The law said, ‘Do not accept a bribe, for a bribe blinds those who see’ (Exodus 23:8). Ezekiel also condemned shepherds who fed on the flock instead of feeding it (Ezekiel 34:2-3).
passages.asks: Micah asks the leaders whether they should not know justice. Ask where you have authority over others, however small, and whether you use it to protect or to take. And ask whose cry you have learned not to hear.

passages.t: Prophets for hire, and a prophet filled with power
passages.happening:
The LORD speaks against ‘the prophets who lead My people astray, who proclaim peace while they chew with their teeth’ (verse 5), and declare war on anyone who does not feed them. So night will come on them without visions, and darkness without divination. The sun will set on these prophets (verse 6). The seers will be ashamed and cover their mouths, because there is no answer from God (verse 7).

‘As for me, however, I am filled with power by the Spirit of the LORD, with justice and courage, to declare to Jacob his transgression and to Israel his sin’ (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Prophets were often supported by gifts from those who consulted them, which made it tempting to tell paying clients what they wanted to hear. As long as they were fed, the message was peace, shalom. Anyone who did not pay heard war.

Divination meant ways of finding out the future, such as reading omens, which the law forbade. By linking the prophets with diviners, Micah treats them as no better than fortune tellers. Covering the mouth was a sign of shame or mourning.

Verse 8 is one of the strongest statements of a prophet's calling in the Bible. Micah contrasts himself with the hired prophets. He is filled not with food but with power, by the Spirit of the LORD, with justice and courage, to name sin.
passages.later: Saul's servant assumed a seer would need a gift before he spoke (1 Samuel 9:7-8), and the law forbade divination (Deuteronomy 18:10-14). Jeremiah faced prophets who said ‘Peace, peace,’ when there was no peace (Jeremiah 6:14).
passages.asks: The hired prophets preached peace to anyone who fed them. Ask whether you have ever softened the truth to keep someone's favor. And Micah was filled with justice and courage. Ask what it would take for you to speak plainly about sin, beginning with your own.

passages.happening:
‘Now hear this, O leaders of the house of Jacob and rulers of the house of Israel, who despise justice and pervert all that is right’ (verse 9), ‘who build Zion with bloodshed and Jerusalem with iniquity’ (verse 10).

‘Her leaders judge for a bribe, her priests teach for a price, and her prophets practice divination for money’ (verse 11). Yet they lean on the LORD and say that he is among them, so no disaster can come. ‘Therefore, because of you, Zion will be plowed like a field, Jerusalem will become a heap of rubble, and the temple mount a wooded ridge’ (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
All three offices are for sale. Leaders were to judge without bribes, priests to teach the law freely, and prophets to speak God's word whatever the reward. Each has turned service into a trade. To build Zion with bloodshed may mean building projects done with forced labor or on property seized from the poor.

Their confidence is the worst of it. They quote their faith as a guarantee, that the LORD is among them. Micah's answer is that the temple they trust will become a wooded hill.

This verse had a remarkable afterlife. About a century later, when Jeremiah was on trial for predicting the temple's fall, elders defended him by quoting Micah 3:12 and recalling that Hezekiah did not put Micah to death but feared the LORD and sought his favor, so that God relented. Jerusalem was spared in 701 BC. The warning was not canceled: the city and temple fell to Babylon in 587 or 586 BC.
passages.later: The elders at Jeremiah's trial said, ‘Micah the Moreshite prophesied in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah’ (Jeremiah 26:18), and quoted this verse word for word.
passages.hard:
If Micah said Zion would be plowed like a field and it did not happen in his lifetime, was he wrong?

Jeremiah 26:17-19 gives the Bible's own answer. The elders recalled that Hezekiah answered Micah's warning with repentance, and the LORD relented from the disaster he had pronounced. On this reading Micah's prophecy was a real warning that achieved its purpose, as Jonah's did in Nineveh. The judgment was delayed, not canceled; Jerusalem fell to Babylon in 587 or 586 BC when later generations returned to the same sins. Some interpreters add that prophecies of judgment often carry a condition even when it is not stated (Jeremiah 18:7-10).

The episode shows that biblical prophecy is not fortune telling but a word meant to change the people who hear it.
passages.asks: The leaders were sure God was with them while they sold justice. Ask whether you have ever used God's presence as a guarantee rather than a call. And ask what it would mean to hear a warning and turn, as Hezekiah did.
